input: Pervaporation is a membrane separation process in which a liquid feed is brought into contact with one side of a membrane, while a vacuum applied to the other side draws the permeating component through the membrane as a vapour. In this study, two membranes are compared for the separation of a feed containing 85 wt% n-butanol in water at 60 °C. The flux, which is defined as the mass permeating per unit membrane area per hour (kg m-2 h-1), and the separation factor, defined as the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed, are used as the measures of performance. The polymer membrane achieved a flux of 1.8 kg m-2 h-1 with a separation factor of 180, although its flux fell by 8% over 500 h of operation. The zeolite membrane, by contrast, gave a flux of 1.3 kg m-2 h-1 and a separation factor of 320, and its flux remained unchanged over 500 h within the limits of measurement error. It should be noted that only one feed composition was tested and that no test was run beyond 500 h. Flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for the same membrane, and the comparison presented here brings the three properties together for the two membranes under the same feed conditions of 85 wt% n-butanol in water at 60 °C, while the stability of either membrane beyond 500 h remains entirely untested.
target: Pervaporation is a membrane separation in which a liquid feed contacts one side of a membrane and vacuum on the other side draws the permeating component through as vapour. Two membranes are compared on a feed of 85 wt% n-butanol in water at 60 °C. Flux is the mass permeating per unit membrane area per hour (kg m-2 h-1), and the separation factor is the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed (dimensionless). The polymer membrane gave a flux of 1.8 kg m-2 h-1 and a separation factor of 180; its flux fell 8% over 500 h. The zeolite membrane gave a flux of 1.3 kg m-2 h-1 and a separation factor of 320, with flux unchanged over 500 h within measurement error. The zeolite membrane is the more selective and the more stable of the two; the polymer membrane passes more mass per unit area per hour. The two membranes divide the performance between them: neither leads on every measure, and the choice between them turns on whether the duty is limited by throughput or by product purity and by the working life expected of the membrane. Flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for one membrane, and the pair of results supplies all three on one feed. The comparison rests on one feed composition and on tests capped at 500 h: the ordering of the two membranes is established at 85 wt% and 60 °C, and stability beyond 500 h is not covered by either result.
